rules: Every entry cites at least one primary source under an https URL.
A reviewed entry records who checked the facts and when; an unreviewed entry stays draft.
An entry never claims that this site protects a wallet or proves a key safe.
A local checker only reads data the user supplies in this browser and never sends an address anywhere.
A vulnerable-key directory is never published: it is a target list, not a safety tool.

checkers.title: Milk Sad seed-range scan
checkers.description: Reproduces bx-seed wallets from a 32-bit MT19937 seed in this tab and compares only the public Bitcoin address the user supplies. The scan makes no network request.
checkers.honesty: A no-match result covers only the seed range entered. The weak set spans 2^32 seeds, so a bounded scan cannot prove a key is safe.

advisories.title: Milk Sad: weak entropy in libbitcoin-explorer bx seed
advisories.summary: libbitcoin-explorer 3.x generated the seed material behind its bx seed command with a Mersenne Twister PRNG seeded by 32 bits of system time. Instead of a 256-bit key space, a wallet made from that output has about 2^32 possible seeds. Anyone who guesses the generation time can reproduce the same wallet.
advisories.user_impact: A Bitcoin wallet whose seed came from an affected bx seed version can be regenerated by someone else and its funds can be swept. A key created with a proper operating-system CSPRNG is not affected by this bug, and an idle vulnerable key cannot be protected by watching it.

tools: wallets or services that generated keys from bx seed output

actions: If a wallet was created with libbitcoin-explorer 3.x or a service that used its bx seed output, create a new wallet with a reputable CSPRNG and a fresh seed phrase.
Move the funds to the new wallet as soon as possible, starting with the highest-value addresses.
Do not reuse the old seed phrase after moving the funds; treat the old key as public.
Use the official Milk Sad research and its checker for the exact affected versions and test vectors.
Use the local seed-range scan on this site only for an address you control; it reproduces keys in this tab and sends nothing.

review.notes: Summary, affected tool and actions checked against the Milk Sad research page and the NVD record on 2026-11-22. Exact patched versions are delegated to the primary sources rather than restated.

advisories.title: Android SecureRandom weakness in wallets created in 2013
advisories.summary: Android builds before 4.4 (API 19) could return predictable output from the platform SecureRandom implementation. Bitcoin wallet apps that generated keys on an affected device could therefore produce keys that another device could also produce. The failure is in the platform random-number generator, not in secp256k1 or in a correctly seeded wallet.
advisories.user_impact: A wallet created on an affected Android device in 2013 may share its key with someone else. The risk depends on the device, the Android version and the wallet app; an address alone does not reveal how its key was generated, so this site cannot run a local check for it.

tools: Android apps using the platform SecureRandom before Android 4.4 (API 19)
Bitcoin wallet apps that generated keys on those devices in 2013

actions: If a wallet was created on an Android device before Android 4.4 in 2013, create a new wallet on a device with a current, patched operating system.
Move the funds to the new wallet; do not keep relying on the old key.
Update the device or wallet app if it is still in use, and read the original bitcoin.org alert for the affected wallet versions.
Treat this entry as history for old wallets; a wallet created today with a current OS and a proper CSPRNG is not affected by this 2013 platform bug.

review.notes: Platform scope and disclosure date checked against the NVD record and the bitcoin.org alert on 2026-11-22. No local checker is claimed because an address cannot show which RNG produced its key.

threats.title: Address poisoning and dusting
threats.summary: An attacker sends a tiny amount of a token or coin from an address chosen to look like one the victim already uses: the same first and last characters, often the same length. The fake address then appears in the victim's transaction history. When the victim later copies an address from history instead of checking it, the transfer goes to the attacker.
threats.user_impact: Funds sent to the lookalike address are lost to the attacker. This is a social-engineering trick, not a break of the wallet software or of the key: no patch fixes it, and a wallet cannot prove that an address is the one the user intended.
actions: Verify the whole address before sending, not only the first and last four characters.
Use an address book or a saved contact for repeat payments; never copy a counterparty from transaction history.
Treat unexpected tiny incoming transfers as untrusted data and ignore them.
Check the destination on a block explorer and confirm it matches the address you intended to pay.
Do not interact with tokens or approvals that arrive from addresses you do not recognise.

sources.label: Etherscan Information Center: address poisoning attacks

review.notes: Kept in the threats section because it is a scam technique with no affected version and no patch; it must never read like a CVE for wallet software. Source URL and topic checked live on 2026-11-22.
